passage:
In Wai, a small town near Satara, Nitin had helped Hafsa's family set up their bangle stall at every temple fair for six years. They'd studied together at the town library, shared rides on his old scooter, and once walked home in the rain laughing for an hour.
Then, at this year's fair, they argued over money from a joint stall they'd tried running. Hafsa said he'd been careless. He shouted that she'd always thought she was better than him. Neither called the other for a month.
Now, when his mother asked about Hafsa, Nitin's jaw tightened. "That friendship was fake from the beginning."
His mother set down the tea. "The girl who sat up with you when your father was in hospital? Fake?"
Nitin looked away. The shouting at the fair was all he could hear.

qa.q: For how many years had Nitin helped set up the bangle stall?
qa.a: Six years, at every temple fair.

qa.q: Why does Nitin now say the friendship was fake from the beginning?
qa.a: The angry argument at the fair is the most intense and most recent memory, so it drowns out six years of study, rides and kindness.

qa.q: What small step could Nitin take while he is still angry?
qa.a: Before deciding the friendship was fake, recall a few of the good years, and later tell Hafsa what hurt him at the fair.

qa.q: How does Nitin's mother see his words?
qa.a: She sees them as unfair to Hafsa, remembering that Hafsa sat up with him when his father was in hospital.

grounding: It shows a young man letting one angry quarrel at the end overwrite six years of friendship.

passage:
Tariq had worked at the secondhand bookshop in Manchester since he was eighteen. Three years of rainy Saturdays sorting paperbacks, reading poetry aloud to the regulars, and being trusted to lock up alone. The old owner had even framed his handwritten shelf labels.
Then the shop was sold, the new manager, Liam, cut his hours, and on his final Friday they argued in front of a customer about the cash count. Tariq slammed the door on his way out.
At the café that evening his friend Ada asked, "Will you miss it?"
"Miss it? It was a dead-end job. Three years wasted."
Ada frowned. "You used to say it was the best place you'd ever worked."
Tariq stared into his cup. He couldn't find that feeling anywhere now. Only the slam of the door.

qa.q: What had the old owner framed?
qa.a: Tariq's handwritten shelf labels.

qa.q: Why can't Tariq find his good feeling about the bookshop now?
qa.a: The argument and the slammed door were the last and most intense moments, so they overwrite three years he once loved.

qa.q: What could Tariq do once he has cooled down?
qa.a: Remember the job in parts, the regulars, the trust, the labels, and keep those years separate from the new manager and the bad last Friday.

qa.q: How might the regulars remember Tariq?
qa.a: As the person who read them poetry on rainy Saturdays, not as someone who slammed the door.

grounding: It shows a young man letting an angry final day at a job overwrite three good years.

passage:
On her last Saturday at the community library in Dehradun, Alka, twenty-one, returned her key at the front desk without looking up. For three years she had run the children's reading hour there. She had built the reading corner from donated cushions and knew every child's favourite book.
But two weeks ago, Jasleen, the head librarian, had accused her in front of volunteers of losing the fee register. It turned up the next day in the cupboard. Jasleen apologised, but Alka had already given notice.
"Three wasted years," she told the security guard. "I don't know why I stayed."
A small boy ran up with a crayon card that said THANK YOU ALKA DIDI. She took it, said "thanks", and pushed it into her bag.
"You were happy here once," the guard said.
"Was I?" She honestly couldn't remember.

qa.q: What had Jasleen accused Alka of losing?
qa.a: The fee register.

qa.q: Why does Alka feel the three years were wasted?
qa.a: The public accusation was the most intense moment and it came at the end, so her anger now covers the reading hours, the reading corner and the children she loved.

qa.q: What could Alka do later, once the anger has settled?
qa.a: She could look back at the whole three years, maybe starting with the crayon card, and let the reading corner and the children count alongside the bad ending.

qa.q: How might the small boy feel when Alka pushes his card into her bag?
qa.a: He may feel a little let down, having made the card for the didi who ran his reading hour, and not understanding why she seems cold.

grounding: It shows a young adult remembering a job by its angriest moment and its last days, so the ending overwrites years of good.

Dear Ganga di,
You asked why I didn't go to Mihir's send-off before he left for Pune. Short answer: we're not friends anymore.
At his farewell dinner last week, in front of everyone, he said I only ever called him when I needed notes. I lost it. I told him he'd always been fake. He walked out.
Since then I keep thinking the whole friendship was fake. Nine years, and it turns out he thought that about me the whole time.
Ammi says, "Tushar, the boy who sat with you all night when Abbu was in hospital? That boy?" Yes, fine, that happened. And the cycling trips, and he taught me to swim. But the dinner is what I see when I close my eyes.
I'm not going to reply to his message. What's the point? It ended the way it ended.
Your brother,
Tushar

qa.q: What did Mihir say at the farewell dinner?
qa.a: He said Tushar only ever called him when he needed notes.

qa.q: Why does Tushar feel the whole nine-year friendship was fake?
qa.a: The angry dinner is the most intense and the latest memory, so it overwrites the night in hospital, the cycling trips and the swimming lessons.

qa.q: What choice could Tushar make instead of ignoring Mihir's message?
qa.a: He could read the message and reply once things have cooled, remembering the nine years as a whole rather than letting one angry evening decide.

qa.q: How might Mihir be feeling now, having sent a message after the fight?
qa.a: Mihir may regret what he said and hope to repair things before he settles in Pune, and could feel hurt if the message is ignored.

grounding: It shows a young adult remembering a friendship by its angry final evening, so the ending overwrites years of good.

passage: Avni, you keep saying your whole internship was awful because of that last fight with your manager. Sit, and let your Mahima maasi tell you something. At twenty-one, I worked two years at a sari shop in Surat. The owner, old Desai-ji, taught me everything: how to read cloth, how to talk to customers, how to count stock. Then on my last day we fought over a missing bundle, and he shouted that I was careless. I left crying, and for years I told everyone that job was hell. Then one day, in my own shop, I caught myself folding a Patola exactly the way Desai-ji taught me, and explaining the weave to a customer in his words. I stood there with the sari in my hands. Two good years, and I had let one angry afternoon write the whole story. I went back and thanked him.

qa.q: Where did Mahima work at twenty-one?
qa.a: Mahima worked at a sari shop in Surat.

qa.q: Why did young Mahima call the job 'hell' for years?
qa.a: Mahima felt hurt and angry after being shouted at on the last day, and that intense ending overwrote two years of learning.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Maasi's story?
qa.a: Catching herself folding a Patola and explaining the weave in Desai-ji's words, which reminded her how much he had taught her, so she went back to thank him.

qa.q: How might Desai-ji have felt when Mahima came back to thank him?
qa.a: Desai-ji might have felt surprised and touched, and perhaps sorry about the last-day quarrel.

grounding: Shows a young woman letting an angry last day overwrite two good years at a job until something brings the whole picture back.

passage: The argument happened on platform 4 at the Delhi station, with six minutes before Ritu's train home. Kunal had forgotten, again, that he had promised to help carry her trunk, and turned up late and defensive. Words flew: "You never show up," "You're so dramatic." The whistle blew. Ritu dragged the trunk on alone, and the door closed on Kunal's face. On the long ride to Jaipur she scrolled through three years of photos and deleted them one by one. Selfish from the start, she thought. Somewhere past midnight, she stopped at one she couldn't delete: Kunal asleep on a hospital bench, the night her father had his surgery. He had sat there eleven hours. Ritu held the phone to her chest. The shouting was real. So were the eleven hours. She didn't restore the photos yet, but she stopped deleting.

qa.q: How long did Kunal sit on the hospital bench?
qa.a: He sat there eleven hours.

qa.q: Why did Ritu start deleting three years of photos?
qa.a: Ritu felt furious and hurt after the platform fight, and that intense final moment made the whole friendship seem selfish from the start.

qa.q: What could Ritu do now that she has stopped deleting?
qa.a: Let the anger cool, remember both the fight and the eleven hours, and talk to Kunal when calmer before deciding about the friendship.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel as the train door closed?
qa.a: Kunal might feel guilty and defensive at once, left on the platform after a fight about something he forgot again.

grounding: Shows a young adult letting an angry ending at a train station overwrite years of friendship, until one memory interrupts it.

passage: At a café near Indiranagar metro, Chandrika stirred her cold coffee hard. "That place was toxic. Eighteen months of my life, wasted." Her last week at the start-up had ended with a shouting match in the exit meeting, her manager calling her ungrateful in front of HR. Farhan, who had joined the same week, raised an eyebrow. "Wasted? You led the app launch. You got that promotion in March. You told me the Goa offsite was the best week of your life." "That was before." "It was all real, though. Just because the last day was awful..." "It was the worst." "It was the loudest," Farhan said. Chandrika looked at her glass. She remembered launch night, everyone cheering in the office. Then the exit meeting pushed back in. "I'm still angry," she said. "Be angry at the manager," Farhan said. "Not at eighteen months."

qa.q: How long did Chandrika work at the start-up?
qa.a: She worked there for eighteen months.

qa.q: Why does Chandrika now call the whole job toxic?
qa.a: Chandrika feels angry and hurt after the shouting match in the exit meeting, and that intense ending is colouring all eighteen months.

qa.q: What is useful about Farhan's advice to be angry at the manager, not at eighteen months?
qa.a: It separates the one bad ending from the whole job, so Chandrika can keep the launch, the promotion and the skills while still being upset about the exit.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Chandrika's time at the start-up?
qa.a: Farhan sees real achievements and happy times, like the launch and the offsite, and a painful last day that was loud rather than typical.

grounding: Shows a young adult letting an angry exit meeting overwrite eighteen good months at a job.

passage: I worked at the bookshop in Kochi for two years during college. I'm Naveen, and when I left last month, I told everyone it was a terrible job. The last week was awful. The owner, Uma chechi, shouted at me for a stock mistake that wasn't mine, and I left without saying goodbye. For weeks I only remembered that shouting. Then I found my old notebook. Uma chechi teaching me how to recommend books. The rainy afternoon when she made ginger tea for all of us. My best day, when a little girl came back to tell me she loved the book I suggested. Two years, and one bad week. I'd let the ending eat everything. Yesterday I went back and said thank you. She looked surprised, then said, "I was wrong about the stock, Naveen. I'm sorry."

qa.a: For two years during college.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling during the weeks after leaving?
qa.a: Naveen felt hurt and bitter, remembering only the shouting in the last week.

qa.q: What did Naveen do after finding the notebook, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: Naveen went back to say thank you, which let the good years count and gave Uma chechi a chance to apologise.

qa.q: How did Uma chechi react when Naveen returned?
qa.a: She looked surprised, then admitted she was wrong about the stock and apologised.

Mentor's note, career guidance session, 5 October.
Mehak came in to talk about her six-month internship at the design studio, which ended in September. She said it was "a total waste" and she never wants to work in design again. When I asked why, she described only the last week: a heated argument with her supervisor, Tushar, over a missed deadline, and leaving without a reference.
I asked her to walk me through month by month. Month one, she led her first client presentation. Month three, her logo was chosen for a national campaign. Month five, Tushar praised her in front of the whole team. She paused. "Those were the best months of my life," she said, surprised.
Next step: she will write to Tushar to close the internship properly and ask for a fair reference.

qa.q: How long was Mehak's internship?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she called the internship a total waste?
qa.a: She felt angry and hurt about the last-week argument, which had overwritten the good months.

qa.q: What is Mehak's next step, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Writing to Tushar to close the internship properly and ask for a fair reference, so the ending doesn't erase six good months.

passage:
Saturday night.
Last shift at the bakery today. Two years, gone. And it ended with Kiran shouting at me over the cash drawer being short by two hundred rupees, in front of customers. I shouted back. I took off my apron and left without saying bye to anyone.
Right now, if you asked me, I'd say those two years were a waste. Worst job, worst boss.
But writing that, I have to be honest with this diary. Kiran gave me the job when I had no experience. Taught me to make croissants at 5 a.m. Covered my shifts when Nani was in hospital. Gave me a birthday cake with my name spelt wrong, which we laughed about for weeks.
Two years of that, and twenty minutes of shouting. Why are the twenty minutes the part I can see so clearly?
Maybe tomorrow I'll send Kiran a message. Not about the cash drawer. About the croissants.
Yash

qa.q: By how much was the cash drawer short?
qa.a: The cash drawer was short by two hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why does Yash call the two years a waste right now?
qa.a: Yash feels angry and humiliated after the shouting, and that intense final twenty minutes overwrites two years of good memories.

qa.q: What does Yash plan, and why is it a good idea?
qa.a: Sending Kiran a message about the croissants, which remembers the whole two years rather than only the fight.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel after the last shift?
qa.a: Kiran may feel upset and regretful too, having taught and supported Yash for two years before the quarrel.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose angry last shift threatens to overwrite two good years at a job.

passage:
Deepika's last day at the small cooperative bank in Karjat ended badly. A farmer's loan file had gone missing, and Keerthana, the branch manager, scolded her in front of the whole queue. The file turned up in the wrong drawer an hour later. Keerthana muttered sorry, but Deepika left without a goodbye.
On the bus home, she decided the job had been miserable from the start. Two wasted years.
Her younger brother, sitting beside her, scrolled through her old photos. "Miserable? Here's you at the branch Diwali party. Here's the farmer who brought you a whole jackfruit because you helped his daughter open an account. Here's Keerthana teaching you the ledger when you started."
Deepika looked. She remembered the jackfruit. She remembered laughing over the ledger.
"One bad hour," her brother said. "You're letting it eat two years."
She stayed quiet till her stop. Then she typed a message to Keerthana: Thank you for teaching me the ledger.

qa.q: Where did the missing loan file turn up?
qa.a: The file turned up in the wrong drawer an hour later.

qa.q: Why did Deepika decide the job had been miserable from the start?
qa.a: Deepika felt humiliated and angry after being scolded in front of the queue, and that final hour coloured two years.

qa.q: What did Deepika do after looking at the photos, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Deepika thanked Keerthana for teaching the ledger, recognising two good years instead of letting one hour define them.

qa.q: How does Deepika's brother see the two years?
qa.a: Deepika's brother sees good times in the photos and warns that one bad hour is eating two years.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose angry last day at a job threatens to overwrite two good years, until old photos bring them back.

Autumn leaves were piling up outside the laundrette in Lisbon when Camila's message came: the café was turning ten, and old staff were invited.
Amara's thumb hovered, then typed: "No thanks. Worst job of my life."
Camila called straight away. "Worst? You were there three years!"
"You saw my last shift. Senhor Duarte shouting at me in front of customers about the grinder, which I didn't even break. I walked out shaking."
"I saw it. It was unfair. But he also covered your shifts for a month when your mum was in hospital. And who taught you latte art? Who gave us those Christmas lunches?"
Amara went quiet. Those memories were there, but faint, like photos left in the sun. The shouting was still loud.
"I'll think about it," she said, still angry, but less sure.

qa.q: How long did Amara work at the café?
qa.a: Amara was there three years.

qa.q: Why does "worst job of my life" feel true to Amara?
qa.a: The unfair shouting on her last shift was both the most intense moment and the ending, so she still feels angry and humiliated, and three years of kindness look faint beside it.

qa.q: What would you advise Amara before she answers Camila?
qa.a: She could write down both the last shift and the good things Camila listed, like the covered shifts and the latte art, and decide about the party with all three years in view.

qa.q: How does Camila see Amara's time at the café?
qa.a: Camila agrees the last shift was unfair but remembers covered shifts, latte art and Christmas lunches, so to her it was far from the worst job.
